title: Portfolio, Career Preparation, and Next Steps
summary: Skills get you hired only if others can see them. This final day focuses on presenting your work: a clean GitHub portfolio with well-documented projects, a resume and LinkedIn tuned for AI roles, and interview preparation covering ML concepts, coding
content:
# Portfolio, Career Preparation, and Next Steps ##### Forty-five days ago On day one you were asked to draw the ML lifecycle and label which tools apply at each stage. That was the whole exercise — no code, just a diagram. Today you have a deployed, monitored, documented AI system with a public URL, built through Python, NumPy, Pandas, SQL, statistics, classical ML, deep learning, transformers, LLM APIs, RAG, Docker, cloud deployment, MLOps and responsible AI practice. The gap between those two points is real. What remains is a translation problem: **converting what you can do into something an employer can recognize in ninety seconds.** That is what this final day is about, and it is a genuinely different skill from the forty-four that preceded it. ##### What a portfolio must prove Hiring managers screen quickly. A portfolio that survives the first pass answers four questions immediately: 1. **Can they ship?** Is there something running that I can click? 2. **Can they think?** Did they choose an approach and justify it? 3. **Can they measure?** Are there numbers, before and after? 4. **Can they communicate?** Can I understand this in two minutes? Three to five projects is right — quality decisively beats quantity. Aim for coverage rather than repetition: - **The capstone** — end to end, deployed, monitored. Your flagship. - **A classical ML project** — tabular data, proper evaluation, feature engineering. - **A deep learning or LLM project** — CNN, fine-tuned transformer, or a RAG application. - **Optionally, a data or MLOps piece** — a pipeline, a CI/CD setup, a monitoring dashboard. Five near-identical Kaggle notebooks demonstrate one skill five times. One deployed system plus one careful analysis plus one fine-tuned model demonstrates three. ##### The README that gets read Your README is the interface to your work. Lead with problem and result, never with the tech stack. ```markdown # Support Ticket Triage *Routes support tickets by category and urgency — macro-F1 0.87, p95 latency 84 ms* 🔗 **Live demo:** https://ticket-triage-xyz.run.app/docs 🎥 **3-min walkthrough:** [link] 💻 **Stack:** Python · XGBoost · FastAPI · Docker · Cloud Run · GitHub Actions ## Problem Agents spent ~3 minutes triaging each of ~400 daily tickets — roughly 20 hours a week of skilled time spent on routing rather than resolution. ## Results | Metric | Baseline | Model | |---|---|---| | Macro-F1 | 0.34 | **0.87** | | Triage time per ticket | 3 min | ~20 s (review only) | | Auto-routed (confidence ≥ 0.75) | — | 71% | | Running cost | — | ₹340/month at 12k requests | ## Architecture [diagram] ## Key decisions - **XGBoost over a fine-tuned transformer**: 0.87 vs 0.89 F1, but 40× faster inference and no GPU. Two points did not justify the cost. - **Confidence gate at 0.75**: calibrated so escalated tickets contain ~85% of the model's errors while sending only 29% to humans. - **Chronological split**: categories shift seasonally; a random split overstated performance by 6 points. ## Limitations - English only; Hindi and Hinglish tickets are escalated by default. - Billing class underperforms (F1 0.71) — only 4% of training data. - Agent corrections are logged but not yet fed back into retraining. ## Run locally \`\`\`bash git clone ... && cd ticket-triage && cp .env.example .env && docker compose up \`\`\` ``` Four elements do the work. **A live link** — clickable beats describable. **A results table with a baseline**, because 0.87 means nothing without knowing that 0.34 was the alternative. **Key decisions with rejected alternatives**, which is engineering judgment made visible. And **honest limitations**, which is counterintuitive and disproportionately effective — it signals you evaluated your own work, and it means you control the hardest interview question. **Tidy the GitHub profile too.** A profile README linking your best three projects, repositories with descriptions and topics, no notebooks with cleared-but-committed outputs, and no `.env` files. A hiring manager who opens your GitHub and finds structured, documented work has learned more in two minutes than an interview round would tell them. ##### Résumé and LinkedIn The résumé rule for someone entering the field: **projects before skills, impact before activity.** ```text PROJECTS Support Ticket Triage — Deployed ML Service github.com/... | live demo Built and deployed an end-to-end ticket classifier reducing triage time from 3 minutes to 20 seconds (macro-F1 0.87 vs 0.34 baseline), serving 12k requests a month at ₹340. XGBoost, FastAPI, Docker, Cloud Run, GitHub Actions CI/CD, drift monitoring. Document Q&A Assistant — RAG Application github.com/... | live demo RAG system over 200 PDFs with hybrid retrieval and citations; recall@5 improved from 0.61 to 0.88 by switching from fixed-size to structure-aware chunking. Python, sentence-transformers, Chroma, Streamlit. ``` Each entry states **what changed and by how much**. Compare that with "Built a machine learning model using Python and scikit-learn" — which describes activity, not outcome. For **LinkedIn**: a headline naming the role and stack ("AI Engineer | Python, PyTorch, LLMs, MLOps | I build and deploy ML systems"), an About section telling one project's story with its result, and Featured links to your capstone and demo. Drop "aspiring" — you have deployed a production service. ##### Interview preparation Four rounds are typical, and each rewards different preparation. **Conceptual.** Bias-variance, overfitting and its fixes, precision versus recall and when each matters, how gradient descent works, why transformers replaced RNNs, what data leakage is, how to handle class imbalance, regularization, cross-validation strategies, and what happens when a model degrades in production. **Coding.** Usually Python and Pandas rather than hard algorithms — group and aggregate a DataFrame, implement a metric from scratch, debug a broken training loop. Practise writing code without an autocomplete crutch. **Project deep-dive.** The most important round, and the most predictable. Prepare a 90-second and a 5-minute version of your capstone, structured as problem → decisions → results → what you would change. **Case/design.** "How would you build a system to detect fraudulent transactions?" Structure beats brilliance here: ```text 1. Clarify volume, latency, cost of false positives vs false negatives, is labelled data available, how quickly do labels arrive? 2. Data sources, features, point-in-time correctness, leakage risks 3. Baseline simplest thing that works — rules, or logistic regression 4. Model approach and why; how you would evaluate 5. Serving real-time or batch, latency budget, confidence thresholds 6. Monitor drift, delayed labels, retraining trigger, rollback 7. Risks class imbalance, adversarial adaptation, fairness ``` **Asking clarifying questions before designing is the strongest signal you can send.** A candidate who asks "how quickly do fraud labels arrive, and what does a false positive cost the customer?" has already demonstrated more than one who starts naming algorithms. Three behavioural questions worth rehearsing: *tell me about a project that did not work* (have one, and describe what you learned), *how do you decide between a simple and a complex model* (the XGBoost-over-transformer reasoning), and *what would you do differently* (your limitations section, spoken). ##### A 60-second self-introduction Structure it as: who you are, one concrete proof, what you are looking for. > *"I'm an AI engineer focused on taking models from notebooks into production. Most recently I built a support ticket triage system — an XGBoost classifier behind a FastAPI service on Cloud Run, with drift monitoring and a CI pipeline. It cut triage time from three minutes to about twenty seconds per ticket, macro-F1 0.87 against a 0.34 baseline, running at around ₹340 a month. What I enjoyed most was the deployment side — the confidence gating and monitoring, deciding which predictions to trust automatically and which to escalate. I'm looking for a role where I can keep working end to end rather than only on modelling."* Roughly 55 seconds. It states a specialization, proves it with a numbered result, shows genuine interest in something specific, and ends with what you want. **Rehearse it aloud until it is comfortable** — reading it silently is not the same, and the difference is audible. ##### Ten concepts to review before interviewing 1. **Bias-variance tradeoff** — and diagnosing which you have from a learning curve. 2. **Overfitting** — causes and the full list of fixes. 3. **Precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC** — and when each is the right metric. 4. **Cross-validation strategies** — stratified, grouped, time-series, and why each exists. 5. **Data leakage** — target, temporal, train-test contamination, and how pipelines prevent it. 6. **Class imbalance** — class weights, SMOTE inside the CV loop, threshold tuning. 7. **Gradient descent and backpropagation** — including vanishing gradients. 8. **Attention and transformers** — why they parallelize where RNNs cannot. 9. **RAG** — chunking, embeddings, retrieval, and why grounding reduces hallucination. 10. **Model degradation** — data drift versus concept drift, detection, and retraining strategy. Add a personal eleventh: **your own projects**. Being unable to explain a decision in your own repository is the worst possible outcome, and it happens. Re-read your code the night before. ##### Specialization paths ```mermaid flowchart TD A[AI Engineer foundations
Python · ML · deployment] --> B{Where next?} B --> C[GenAI / LLM Engineer
RAG, agents, evals, fine-tuning] B --> D[MLOps / Platform
pipelines, infra, monitoring] B --> E[Computer Vision
detection, segmentation, edge] B --> F[NLP Engineer
IE, multilingual, search] B --> G[Data Science
experimentation, causal inference] C & D & E & F & G --> H[Senior / Lead / Staff
or Architect / Consultant] ``` | Path | Focus | India range (2026) | |---|---|---| | **GenAI / LLM Engineer** | RAG, agents, evaluation, prompt systems | ₹12–30L entry, scarce supply | | **MLOps / Platform** | Pipelines, infrastructure, reliability | ₹10–25L | | **Computer Vision** | Detection, segmentation, edge deployment | ₹8–20L | | **NLP Engineer** | Extraction, multilingual, semantic search | ₹8–22L | | **Data Scientist** | Experimentation, causal inference, analytics | ₹8–20L | The honest advice on choosing: **do not specialize immediately.** Take a generalist role, notice which problems you return to voluntarily, and specialize into that after a year. The exception is GenAI, where demand currently exceeds supply substantially enough that entering directly is viable if the work interests you. ##### Staying current The field moves fast enough that specific tools decay. Anchor on what transfers. A cadence that is sustainable beats intensity that is not: ```text Weekly 45 min changelogs (PyTorch, HuggingFace, provider APIs) + one deep read Weekly 3 h build — extend a project or try one new tool Monthly 2 h publish something: a post, a template, a repo Quarterly half day review the growth plan; reassess target roles Yearly one substantial project outside your comfort zone ``` Where to read: **arXiv** (cs.LG, cs.CL) selectively, **Papers with Code** for implementations, the **Hugging Face** and **Google AI** blogs, and Andrej Karpathy's videos for genuinely first-principles explanations. The compounding asset is **public work**. A published article, an open-source contribution, a widely-used template — these generate opportunities passively in a way private excellence never does. One post about a problem you solved will bring more inbound interest than a year of private study. ##### Common mistakes - **Waiting until you feel ready.** You will not. Apply now; readiness comes from interviewing. - **Listing tools instead of outcomes** on the résumé. - **No live demo** — a link outperforms a repository, which outperforms a description. - **A README leading with the tech stack** rather than the problem and result. - **No numbers**, so "improved performance" cannot be evaluated. - **Hiding limitations**, which reads as not having looked for them. - **Unable to explain your own code** in a deep-dive round. - **Designing before clarifying** in a case interview. - **Five similar projects** instead of three varied ones. - **Learning entirely in private**, so nothing compounds. - **Not asking for feedback** after rejections — some interviewers answer, and those answers are worth more than another course. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **polish your GitHub, write strong READMEs, and update your résumé and LinkedIn** to present you as an AI engineer. Work through your repositories and delete or archive the abandoned ones — a profile with four strong projects reads better than one with fourteen where ten are half-finished tutorials. The mini project is your **portfolio page** — a personal site, a Notion page, or a curated GitHub profile — featuring the capstone and two or three best projects with clear write-ups. Then run the real test: send the link to someone outside your field and ask what you do and what you built. If they can explain it back, it works. If they cannot, the problem is your writing, not their attention. For the assignment, **draft a 60-second self-introduction and list ten concepts to review before interviewing**. Record the introduction and play it back — the gap between how it reads and how it sounds is always instructive, and the fix is usually cutting a third of the words. For the concepts, use the list above but personalize it: add whichever topics you found hardest during these 45 days, because those are the ones an interviewer's follow-up question will find. ##### Key takeaways - A portfolio must prove four things quickly: you can ship, think, measure and communicate — three to five varied projects beat many similar ones. - Lead every README with the problem and a measured result, include a live link, justify key decisions against rejected alternatives, and document limitations honestly. - Write the résumé as impact rather than activity — what changed, and by how much. - In case interviews, clarify volume, latency, label availability and error costs before designing; structure beats brilliance. - Specialize after a year of generalist work rather than immediately, keep a sustainable weekly learning cadence, and make your work public so it compounds.
